result.content:
A hash table is a way to store key–value pairs so that a later lookup can find the value associated with a key without scanning every stored item. The central idea is to use a hash function to turn each key into a number that identifies a bucket. A bucket is typically one position in an array maintained by the table, or a small container attached to one position. The hash function must be deterministic: the same key must produce the same bucket number while the table configuration remains unchanged. It should also spread keys as evenly as possible, though real hash functions rarely distribute every possible key perfectly. The bucket number is not the value and is not the key’s meaning; it is a shortcut to the place where the entry may be stored.

When an entry is inserted, the table computes the key’s hash, goes to the corresponding bucket, and stores the key together with its value there. If that bucket is empty, insertion is straightforward. If the bucket already contains an entry, the table has a collision. Collision handling by chaining means that each bucket keeps a chain—often a linked list, although other collections can serve the same purpose—of all entries whose keys hash to that bucket. Each entry in the chain retains its full key and its value, so the table can distinguish between two keys that happen to land in the same bucket. A bucket is therefore not necessarily a single key-value pair; it can be a small collection whose contents must be examined entry by entry.

To find a value, the table receives a lookup key and repeats the same hash calculation that was used during insertion. It goes directly to the resulting bucket, then walks through the entries in that bucket’s chain. For each entry, it compares the stored key with the lookup key using exact equality. If the keys match, the associated value is returned. If the first entry does not match, the lookup continues to the next entry in the chain. If the chain ends without a match, the key is absent. This procedure is why the hash is useful: rather than checking every key in the table, the lookup usually checks only the entries in one bucket, and often only one entry.

A made-up illustration can show the mechanics without claiming to describe a real hash function. Suppose the table has at least six buckets, and, purely for this example, the invented assignments are cedar to bucket 2, maple to bucket 2, and pine to bucket 5. The entries might store cedar with one value, maple with another, and pine with a third. Bucket 2 then contains a chain with cedar and maple, while bucket 5 contains only pine. To look up maple, the table computes the made-up hash for maple and arrives at bucket 2. It examines the chain there: cedar does not match maple, so it moves on; the next entry is maple, and its value is returned. To look up pine, the table goes to bucket 5 and finds pine immediately. The cedar-and-maple collision was normal and was handled by the chain, not by losing either entry. These assignments are explicitly invented for the illustration and should not be read as the output of any particular real hash function.

The load factor is the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. It measures how crowded the table is. If the load factor is small, most buckets contain few entries and chains are short. If it grows too large, many buckets contain longer chains, so a lookup may have to inspect more entries. A hash table typically resizes when the load factor crosses a chosen threshold; for instance, an implementation might use a threshold around 0.75, although actual thresholds vary. Resizing means allocating a larger bucket array and reinserting, or rehashing, every existing entry: each key must be hashed again because its bucket number may change in the new array. The resizing operation itself takes time proportional to the number of entries, since every entry must be moved. It is done only occasionally, and its cost can be spread over many insertions, so the average cost of insertion remains roughly constant. After resizing, the load factor falls and the chains are likely to become shorter again.

For a well-designed hash function and a controlled load factor, lookup has expected constant-time behavior. In ordinary terms, the expected number of entries inspected is a small constant that does not grow with the number of stored items, because the expected chain length is approximately the load factor. A lookup still performs a fixed amount of work to compute the hash and select the bucket, and then only a short chain is expected. This is an average over the likely distribution of keys, not a promise for every possible key. The worst case is different. If a poor hash function sends many keys to the same bucket, or if an adversary deliberately chooses keys that collide, chaining puts all those entries in one long chain. A lookup for a key in that chain may have to compare against every entry, so the time becomes linear in the number of entries. The distinction matters because a hash table’s practical speed depends on assumptions about hash quality, key distribution, and load factor; if those assumptions fail, the structure can degenerate into long chains. Thus hash tables offer expected constant-time lookup in normal use, while their worst-case lookup can be linear when collisions are extreme. That is how the lookup finds its way.
